column1: # The ideas the pages explain simply (lesson::eli5): id, the term, the explanation, then optionally a worked example and the slug of the lesson that teaches it. Tab-separated. A page links a word to its id; the reader opens it.

column3: A language model is a program that continues text: you give it some words and it works out what could come next. Nobody wrote its rules by hand; it was shaped by being shown a huge amount of text. What it learned is stored as numbers.

A weight is one of the numbers inside a model. Picture a mixing desk with billions of little knobs: each knob is a weight, and how they are all set decides what the model does. Learning means turning the knobs.
A table is numbers set out in rows and columns, like a spreadsheet with nothing but numbers in it. Mathematicians call it a matrix. "4 x 4" means 4 rows and 4 columns, so 16 numbers.

A model works in steps, like stations on an assembly line. Each station takes a list of numbers, mixes them using its own table of weights, and hands a new list to the next station. One station is a layer.

column2: multiplying a table by a list
column3: Take one row of the table. Multiply each of its numbers by the matching number of the list, and add the results: that gives one number. Do the same for every row and you have a new list, one number for each row. In the lessons it is written as two names side by side, the table first and then the list.
column4: Take the table with rows (1, 2) and (3, 4), and the list (10, 1). Row 1 gives 1 × 10 + 2 × 1 = 12. Row 2 gives 3 × 10 + 4 × 1 = 34. The new list is (12, 34).

column3: A model that already knows a lot is given extra lessons on one particular thing, the way a trained cook learns a new cuisine. The lessons work by nudging its weights. It is adjusting, not starting over.

Training is practice with correction. The model answers, the answer is compared with the one wanted, and the weights are nudged a little so the next answer is closer. Then again, many thousands of times.

For each weight, the gradient says which way to turn that knob, and how hard, to make the answer a little less wrong. Like feeling which way the ground slopes under your feet when you want to walk downhill.

The usual training method does not trust one nudge alone. For each weight it remembers the recent nudges, and how large they were, and moves by that memory. That is two more remembered numbers for every weight being trained.
Write over a page of your notebook and the old notes are gone. What a model knows is in its weights, so changing all of them to learn one new thing can write over what it knew, sometimes badly.
Frozen weights are knobs with tape over them: training is not allowed to turn them. They still do their work every time the model runs. They just never change.

An adapter is a small add-on beside a layer, like a clip-on lens on a camera. The camera is not altered; the lens changes the picture. Only the adapter has numbers that are trained, and it can be taken off again.

LoRA is one way to build an adapter: two thin tables, one that squeezes the input of the layer down to a few numbers, and one that spreads those few back out. What comes out is added to what the layer gives anyway. The name is short for low-rank adaptation.

Rank is how narrow the middle of the adapter is: how many numbers the input is squeezed into before being spread out again. Rank 1 is a single number, like summing up a whole room on one dial. A higher rank lets more through, and needs more numbers.
column4: A layer takes a list of 4 numbers. At rank 1 the adapter first boils those 4 down to 1 number, then spreads that 1 back out to 4. At rank 2 it boils them down to 2 numbers, so more of the input gets through, and it has twice as many numbers of its own.

column3: The number the strength s is set from, chosen before training: a volume knob for the adapter. At 0 the adapter adds nothing and the layer behaves as it did before. Turn it up and whatever the adapter adds counts for more.
column4: If the adapter would add (7, 0, -7, 3.5) at a strength of 2, then at a strength of 1 it adds half of that, and at 0 it adds nothing.

column3: Once training is over, what the adapter adds can be added into a copy of the table of the layer, giving one ordinary table that does the same job, so nothing extra is computed when the model runs. It is a choice, not a must: the original table is still there, and an adapter kept apart can be taken off or swapped for another.

The cost of training goes with how many numbers are being trained. A table with 4096 rows and 4096 columns holds 4096 x 4096 numbers. The two thin tables of an adapter hold only rank x (rows + columns).
column4: A table of 4 rows and 4 columns holds 4 × 4 = 16 numbers. An adapter of rank 1 for it holds 1 × (4 + 4) = 8.

column3: X_eTaL is the small programming language the computations on this page are written in. It is an array language: one short instruction works on a whole list or table of numbers at once, so the code stays close to the mathematics. You do not need to know it: every piece shown here is explained.

X_eTaL reads a line from the right: each word takes everything to its right as its input. So in "B times A times x" the rightmost pair, A times x, is worked out first, and B is then applied to that result.
A function is a named recipe: hand it ingredients and it hands back a result. X_eTaL draws the name of a function with one letter underlined. The signs + and x (times) are functions too.

A library is a box of ready-made, tested functions, like a toolbox. The line that reads "lo:" use< "LoRA" opens the toolbox called LoRA and gives it the short name lo. After that, a name drawn with a small raised lo in front of it means: that tool, from that toolbox.

Several things inside round brackets, with commas between, are handed over together as one bundle. (W, A, B, s) is the layer and its adapter in one bundle: the frozen table, the two thin tables and the strength.

In the code, "multiply a table by a list" is written with three words: a quoted +, a quoted x (times), and inner. Together they say: pair the numbers up, multiply each pair, add the results. The quote mark before + and x hands those two operations over to inner instead of doing them right away.

To find the rank of a table, count how many of its rows say something new, that is, are not just a multiple or a mix of rows already counted. Gram-Schmidt is the standard step-by-step way of doing that count.
Computers keep decimals with tiny rounding errors. "Within 1e-12" means two results agree to 12 decimal places: the same for every practical purpose.
Models are sized by how many weights (also called parameters) they have. Seven billion is a common size for a model that runs on a good laptop or one graphics card.
In the code, the arrow ← gives a value a name: the name is on its left, the value on its right. So "x ← 1 2 3 4" reads: x is the list 1, 2, 3, 4. (It is typed as a colon and an equals sign.)
A line that starts with the sign ⍝ is a note for the reader, not an instruction: the computer skips it. In this program the notes say in words what the lines under them do.
When the program asks a yes-or-no question, such as "are these two results the same?", it prints 1 for yes and 0 for no.

The number the correction is multiplied by before it is added. LoRA sets it to alpha divided by the rank, so that the correction stays about the same size when the rank is changed; lesson 4 shows a second rule for it. In LoRA hello the rank is 1, so there s is alpha itself.
What the adapter adds to the output of the layer. The frozen layer gives its usual answer; the correction is the small list of numbers added on top. Other texts call it the update, or delta.

A list is some numbers in a row, in a fixed order: (1, 2, 3, 4) is a list of four numbers. The lessons give a list a short name, often a single letter such as x, so they can talk about all of its numbers at once.
A stage is one step of a calculation: it takes the numbers worked out so far, does one thing to them, and hands on new numbers. A calculation in four stages is four such steps, one after another.
One input together with the output wanted for it. Training is done on a set of examples: the model's output for each input is compared with the one wanted.
column4: On this page an example is a list of 8 numbers going in and the list of 8 wanted out, made by a layer the adapter never sees.

column3: One number that says how wrong the model is on a set of examples: the differences between its outputs and the ones wanted, squared (so that a miss either way counts, and a large miss counts much more), added up, and halved. Training tries to make it smaller. Zero would mean every output exactly right.
column4: Outputs (1, 2) wanted (1, 4): the differences are 0 and -2, their squares 0 and 4, the sum 4, the loss 2.

column3: Examples kept back from training and used only to measure. The loss on them says whether what was learned carries over to inputs the model has not practiced on, which is the kind it will meet afterward.

How far the weights move on each step of training, as a fraction of what the gradient asks for. Too small and training crawls; too large and each step overshoots, so the loss jumps about instead of falling.

The usual way of taking training steps. Instead of moving by the latest gradient alone, it keeps running averages of the recent gradients and of their sizes for every weight trained, and moves by those, so one unusual step does not throw it off.

When a model fits the examples it trained on more and more closely while getting no better, or worse, on examples it has not seen: it has learned those particular examples rather than what they have in common. Too few examples for the size of what is being trained invites it.

What was written down during training, every so many steps: the loss, and the weights being trained as they were then. A page that has the record can show any point of the training again without training again.

LoRA-FA is LoRA with the first small table, A, frozen: made once from a seed and not trained; only B moves. That halves the numbers to train and the optimizer's memory, and a saved adapter need not store A, since the seed regrows it. The price: every row of the update s B A is a mix of A's rows, so the update can only lie where those rows let it. (Zhang and others, 2023.)

Full fine-tuning moves every number of the layer (or of the whole model) during training, with no adapter: the table W itself changes. Nothing limits what it can reach. Its costs: a gradient for every number, two more numbers of optimizer memory for each, and a whole changed copy of the model to store afterward. Adapters trade some of that reach for smaller costs.
column4: On an 8 by 8 layer it trains all 64 numbers; while it trains, their 64 gradients and Adam's 128 averages are held beside them, 192 more.

column3: A table can be split into rank-1 pieces, largest first; its singular values are the sizes of those pieces. A table of rank 4 has four that are not 0, then zeros. The closest any table of rank k can come to it leaves out the pieces past the k-th, so the lowest loss possible at rank k is half the sum of the squared singular values after the k-th (Eckart and Young, 1936).
column4: A table with singular values 3, 2, 1 and then zeros: at rank 2 the lowest loss possible is half of 1 squared, 0.5; at rank 3 and up it is 0.

column3: Take a few lists of numbers of the same length, the rows of a table say, and all the lists you can make from them by scaling each and adding them up. That collection is a subspace: a flat region, through the origin, inside the space of all lists of that length. Two lists of 8 that do not line up give a flat sheet inside 8-dimensional space. A table's rows make its row space.

A basis of a subspace is a set of lists that span it with none to spare: every point of the subspace is one mix of them, and no list in the set is a mix of the others. The rows of the frozen A are a basis of its row space (when they are independent): each row of the update s B A is a mix of them, with B's numbers as the amounts.

The projection of a list onto a subspace is the point of the subspace nearest to it: drop a perpendicular from the list to the flat region, and the foot of it is the projection. What is left, the list minus its projection, is the remainder; its size says how much of the list lies outside the subspace. A list already in the subspace is its own projection, with a remainder of 0.
column4: On this page each learned update's rows are projected onto the frozen A's row space: LoRA-FA's remainder is 0 to rounding; LoRA's is not, at a rank under 8 (at rank 8 the row space is the whole space).

column3: Retention is what a model keeps of what it did before it learned something new. Here it is a loss: some old inputs are kept, with the outputs the layer gave them before any training, and after training the layer's loss on those old examples says how far it moved from what it did. 0 means nothing changed for them; the larger, the less was kept. It is the measure behind catastrophic forgetting.

The context is the text a language model is given before it answers. Put the new facts or examples there and the model uses them for that answer, with no weight changed; take them away and it is as it was. It costs nothing to train and keeps nothing.

Back-propagation is how the gradient is found: the model's answer is worked out forward, the error at the end is traced back through every step, and each weight gets its share of the blame. It needs each step's input kept until the trace comes back, which is memory, and it needs the loss to be a smooth formula of the weights.

A forward pass is one run of the model from input to answer, nothing traced back. It is the cheap half of training: no memory of the steps kept, no gradient. Methods that learn from forward passes alone try the weights nudged one way and the other and compare the losses.
Selective fine-tuning moves some of the layer's numbers and leaves the rest: chosen rows, chosen layers, or a chosen fraction. Fewer numbers trained than the whole, with the choice made beforehand.

QLoRA is LoRA with the frozen W stored at 4 bits a number instead of 16, a quarter of the bytes. The adapter is trained as LoRA's is, on the unpacked W; the adapter's own count does not change, the base's bytes do.

DoRA splits each column of W into its size (one number) and the column scaled to size 1 (its direction), puts the adapter on the direction, and trains the size apart: one more number per column beside LoRA's tables.

VeRA keeps both tables A and B frozen, grown from a seed and the same for every layer, and trains two short lists of numbers that scale them. Far fewer numbers than LoRA's; the tables are shared, the lists are the task's own.

Instead of tracing the error back, nudge the weights by a random amount, run forward, nudge the other way, run forward, and move toward whichever was less wrong. Only forward passes, no gradient and no memory of the steps; it learns from two losses at a time, so it takes many passes, how many against back-propagation being a thing to measure.

A closed-form edit changes the layer by a formula, once, with no training steps: for one input, make the layer give a chosen output, by adding a rank-one change worked out from the input and the wanted output. Exact for that input; what it does to other inputs is the question.

A language model is given a model's weights, or a way to probe them, proposes a change, applies it to a copy, and tests it. The arithmetic of the change is one of the other families'; what is new is who chooses it. Published so far (November 2026): one small demonstration in a blog post, no paper and no replication yet.

A fine-tuning method answers two questions apart. The first: where may the change to the weights live? In every weight; in two thin tables beside them; in a few numbers scaling fixed tables; in one rank-one edit. The same answer can be found by any of the ways of searching.
The second question: how is the change found? By back-propagation; by forward passes alone; by a formula; by an AI proposing and testing. Any answer here pairs with any place the change may live.
A number in a model is stored at some precision: 32 bits, 16, or fewer. Halve the bits and the bytes halve, with some of each number's detail lost. 4 bits is 16 distinct values per number.

A seed is one whole number that starts a random-number maker; the same seed gives the same random numbers every time. A table grown from a seed need not be stored: the seed regrows it. LoRA-FA's frozen A and VeRA's two shared tables are such tables.

In this course a saga is a group of lessons built together, planned once and then made one lesson at a time. Saga 1 is the LoRA lessons; Saga 2 the variations; Saga 3 shared subspaces; Saga 4 learning without back-propagation; Saga 5 editing weights and an AI doing it.

A skip connection lets a layer add to the list it was given instead of replacing it: the new list is the old one plus a correction. Nothing of the input is thrown away on the way through, so a deep stack of layers still knows what it was given, and a correction of zero changes nothing. Also called a residual connection: the layer only works out what is left to add.
column4: A layer is given (0.96, 0.83, 0.62, ...) and works out a correction (0.07, 0.02, -0.11, ...). Without a skip it hands on the correction alone; with one it hands on the sum, (1.03, 0.85, 0.51, ...).

column3: A stream is one copy of the list a model carries from layer to layer. Ordinary models carry one; Hyper-Connections carry several side by side, here four, so the state between layers is a table of four rows, one row a stream. The layers then also decide how the streams mix.
column4: Four streams of 8 numbers are a 4 x 8 table. At the start all four rows hold the same list; after a layer they differ.

column3: A mixing table says how the streams are combined: a small table (4 x 4 for four streams) whose row s gives the weights for making new stream s out of the old ones. Hyper-Connections have three: one before the block, one for the shares of the block's output, and one for the state carried on.
column4: With row (0.711, 0.096, 0.096, 0.096) the new first stream is 0.711 of the old first stream plus 0.096 of each of the others.

column3: Before the block runs, the four streams are averaged into one list, since the block takes one list of 8, not a table of four. The block's output is then handed back to each stream, each getting its own share of it.
column4: Four rows averaged column by column give one row of 8 numbers.

column3: A mapping that gives back exactly what it was given. A plain skip connection is one: the list goes through unchanged and the layer adds to it. With several streams the state is multiplied by a mixing table instead, and the paper asks that table to keep what the skip kept: each new stream a weighted average of the old ones (rows summing to 1), the streams' total unchanged (columns summing to 1).
column4: A table with rows and columns summing to 1 keeps the streams' total; one with rows summing to 3.82 makes each new stream 3.82 times a weighted average, every layer.

column3: A way of building a deep model that widens the single carried list into several streams and lets each layer learn how to mix them, before and after its block and for the state carried on. Proposed by Zhu and others in 2024. The mixing tables are not held to anything; the mHC paper reports that at scale the carried state can then inflate across many layers.

Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (Xie and others, DeepSeek, 2025): Hyper-Connections with one rule added. The table that mixes the state carried on is replaced, before it is used, by the nearest one whose rows and columns each sum to 1, so that across any depth each stream stays a weighted average and the streams' total is kept.
column4: The table with 2.718 on its diagonal and 0.368 elsewhere (rows summing to 3.82) becomes the one with 0.711 on its diagonal and 0.096 elsewhere (rows and columns summing to 1).

column3: A table of positive numbers whose rows each sum to 1 and whose columns each sum to 1. Multiplying a list by such a table takes a weighted average of its entries, so the result can be no larger than the largest entry and no smaller than the smallest; two such tables multiplied give another.
column4: (0.711 0.096 0.096 0.096) across each row and down each column, in a 4 x 4, sums to 1 both ways.

column3: A way of turning any table of positive numbers into one whose rows each sum to 1 and whose columns each sum to 1: divide every row by its sum, then every column by its sum, and repeat; the sums settle at 1, faster from some starts than from others. Twenty rounds are used here, the paper's count, and lesson D2 shows a start they are not enough for.
column4: From e on the diagonal and 1/e elsewhere, one round gives 0.711 and 0.096; from a lopsided 4 x 4 the rows are within a millionth of 1 after eleven rounds.

column3: Dividing every number in a row of a table by that row's sum, so that the row then sums to 1 and its numbers become shares of the whole. Column normalization is the same down each column. One can undo the other a little: after the columns are made to sum to 1, the rows are off again, by less than before.

A square table with a single 1 in each row and each column and 0 everywhere else. Multiplying a list by it only reorders the list: each row keeps one entry and drops the rest. Birkhoff's theorem (1946) says a doubly stochastic table is a weighted mix of permutation tables, with positive weights summing to 1.
column4: With rows keeping entries 2, 1, 4, 3, the list (a, b, c, d) becomes (b, a, d, c).

column3: The most a table can lengthen any list it multiplies: the ratio of the size of the result to the size of the list, for the list that makes it largest. It is the table's largest singular value. A table with spectral norm at most 1 stretches nothing, and 48 of them in a row stretch nothing either.
column4: A doubly stochastic 4 x 4 has spectral norm 1; e on the diagonal and 1/e elsewhere has 3.82.

column3: A fixed curve applied to each number of a list between a block's two tables: a positive number comes out about as it went in, a negative one comes out close to zero, with a smooth bend between. Without such a curve two tables in a row could do no more than one table; the name is Gaussian Error Linear Unit.

Logits are numbers that are not yet weights: a table of them is turned into weights by a rule, such as a softmax or an exponential, that makes every weight positive and, when wanted, every row sum to 1. A model learns the logits; the rule keeps the weights in bounds whatever the logits become.
column4: The logits (1, -1, -1, -1) put through a softmax are the weights (0.711, 0.096, 0.096, 0.096).

column3: The diagonal of a square table is the run of cells from its top left to its bottom right: row 1 column 1, row 2 column 2, and so on. The identity table, written I, has 1 on its diagonal and 0 everywhere else, and multiplying by it changes nothing; 2I - 1 has 1 on the diagonal and -1 everywhere else.

A rule that turns a row of any numbers into positive weights that sum to 1: raise e to each number, then divide each result by their total. The largest number gets the largest weight, and no weight is ever 0 or 1 exactly.

The exponential of a number is e, 2.718..., raised to it: a positive number for any input, large for large inputs and close to 0 for very negative ones. It is the first step of a softmax, and HC uses it on its own, without the dividing step.
column4: The exponential of 1 is 2.718; of -1, 0.368; of 0, 1.

column3: How much a table multiplies what passes through it, measured as one number. A table applied at many layers multiplies again at each, so a gain a little above 1 grows very large over many layers and one a little below 1 shrinks toward 0. A gain of exactly 1 stays put at any depth.
column4: A gain of 3.82 at each of 12 layers is 3.82 multiplied by itself 12 times, about 9.8 million.

column3: The one table that stands for several layers' tables applied in turn: their product. With the same table H at every layer, the composite of k layers is H multiplied by itself k times, written H^k. The mHC paper measures the composite from a layer to the top of the model.
column4: With H at two layers, the composite is H times H.

column3: The largest of a table's row sums, ignoring signs: the mHC paper's Amax Gain Magnitude on the way forward through the layers. If every number in a list is at most 1 in size, no number of the table times the list can be larger than this.
column4: A table whose rows sum to 3.82, 3.82, 3.82 and 3.82 has forward gain 3.82.

column3: The largest of a table's column sums, ignoring signs: the mHC paper's Amax Gain Magnitude on the way back, when training sends corrections from the last layer toward the first through the same tables. For a table whose rows and columns each sum to 1, it is 1, like the forward gain.
column4: A table whose columns each sum to 1 has backward gain 1.

column3: The measure the Python re-implementation of mHC used for a table's gain, which its code says is not the paper's: the largest single number in the table, given as its power of ten (log10). It is a different number from the paper's Amax gain for the same table.
column4: A table whose largest number is 0.25 has proxy log10 0.25, -0.602.

column3: The size of the whole gradient as one number: the square root of the sum of the squares of its entries, one per weight. It says how hard a training step pushes the weights. A size that jumps by many times from one step to the next, or grows without stopping, is a sign that training has run into trouble; a size near 0 means the steps no longer move anything.
column4: A gradient of 3 and 4 has size 5.

column3: A step of training in which some number came out as NaN (not a number, what 0 divided by 0 gives) or infinite (too large for the computer to hold). Once one appears it spreads through every calculation that uses it, and the training is ruined. Counting them is a plain check that a run stayed within numbers.
column4: A run of 800 steps with no NaN event has a count of 0.

column3: A learned table with one row per token: looking a token up gives its row, the list of numbers the model works on. It is trained like any other weights, so tokens that the task treats alike can end up with similar rows.
column4: With 16 tokens and lists of 8, the embedding is a 16 x 8 table.

column3: A loss for picking one answer among several: minus the logarithm of the chance the model gave the right answer, averaged over the examples. It is 0 when the right answer gets a chance of 1 and grows as that chance falls. Guessing evenly among n answers gives the logarithm of n.
column4: Among 16 answers, guessing evenly gives the logarithm of 16, 2.77.

column3: A slow, simple way to find how the loss changes with one weight: move the weight up by a tiny amount, measure the loss, move it down by the same amount, measure again, and divide the difference by twice the amount. It needs two runs per weight, so it is used to check a gradient worked out by hand, not to train.
column4: Losses of 1.0002 and 0.9998 a millionth either side give a slope of 200.

column3: A run computed beforehand on a computer, by the same program the page shows, because it takes too long to compute while you wait (minutes, where a page has seconds). Its record of every step is saved with the page, along with what made it, so that it can be read back.
column4: At 48 layers each run of 800 steps took about four minutes.

column3: Reading an offline run's saved record back and drawing it, without computing the run again. A replay changes no number: it shows what the run computed, step by step, and a short run on the page checks that the program is the one that made it.
column4: The page's 50 steps match the first 50 of the saved 800.

column3: Mixing tables made afresh for every input, from the stream state the layer is given, instead of learned once and fixed. Two different inputs are then mixed differently. The mHC paper's tables are dynamic; the Python re-implementation's, and the earlier pages', are fixed.
column4: At a gating factor of 0.01, two inputs' H_post weights differ by about 0.02.

column3: A learned number that multiplies the part of a mixing table that comes from the input, before the fixed part (the bias) is added. At 0 the input has no say and the table is fixed; the larger it is, the more the input moves the table. The mHC paper starts it at 0.01.
column4: At 0, every input makes the same tables.

column3: Dividing a list by its root mean square: the square root of the mean of the squares of its numbers. Afterwards the list's root mean square is 1, so what is left is its shape, not its size. RMS stands for root mean square.
column4: The list 3, 4 has mean square 12.5 and root mean square 3.54; divided by it, 0.85 and 1.13.

column3: A learned number, or list of numbers, added after a multiplication, so that the result need not be 0 when the input is 0. In a mixing table it is the part that is the same for every input.
column4: With a bias of 2I - 1 and a gating factor of 0, H_res is the earlier pages' fixed table.

column3: A smooth curve that turns any number into one between 0 and 1: very negative numbers come out near 0, very positive ones near 1, and 0 comes out as one half. The mHC paper puts H_pre's numbers through it, and H_post's through twice it.
column4: The sigmoid of 0 is 0.5; of 2, 0.88.
